# Results — Study 171 (Naive-1-Over-N) on real data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Out-of-sample tournament
of four portfolio strategies on eleven SPDR sector ETFs (XLB, XLC, XLE, XLF, XLI,
XLK, XLP, XLRE, XLU, XLV, XLY). Rolling 60-month estimation window; positions
entered at the start of the following month; one-way rebalance cost 10 bps.
As-of **2026-06-15**; match the fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data.*

## The tournament — lookback=60 months, cost=10 bps one-way

The out-of-sample period (≈ 2023–2026) is the post-lookback slice where all four
strategies' weights are computed from historical data only.

| Strategy | CAGR | Sharpe | Max DD | HAC t (annual) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **1/N (equal-weight)** | **15.12%** | **1.179** | −15.30% | +5.02 |
| Min-Variance | 12.11% | 1.084 | −10.95% | +3.55 |
| Max-Sharpe (Tangency) | 16.56% | 1.111 | −17.64% | +5.81 |
| Mean-Variance (λ=3) | 16.56% | 1.111 | −17.64% | +5.81 |

**Key pairwise differentials (optimiser − 1/N):**

| Matchup | Annual return diff | HAC t | n years |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Min-Var − 1/N | **−2.02%** | **−2.29** | 4 |
| Max-Sharpe − 1/N | +0.96% | +2.62 | 4 |
| MVO − 1/N | +0.96% | +2.62 | 4 |

The verdict is **MIXED**: 1/N beats min-variance on both CAGR and Sharpe (the
Sharpe differential is statistically significant at HAC *t* = −2.29 in 1/N's favour).
Max-Sharpe ekes out a higher raw CAGR (+0.96%) and a better HAC *t* (+2.62), but
*loses* on risk-adjusted return (Sharpe 1.111 vs 1.179). Neither result is convincing
evidence that optimisation reliably beats 1/N — the short out-of-sample window (n=4
annual observations) makes every number fragile to the specific realisation.

## Sensitivity: lookback length (cost=10 bps)

| Lookback | 1/N Sharpe | Min-Var | Max-Sharpe | MVO |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 24 months | 1.019 | 0.957 | 0.795 | 0.795 |
| 36 months | 0.775 | 0.741 | 0.504 | 0.504 |
| 60 months | 1.179 | 1.084 | 1.111 | 1.111 |
| 84 months | 1.851 | 1.228 | 1.675 | 1.675 |

1/N leads on Sharpe across all lookback choices. Its dominance is **robust to the
lookback parameter** — a consistent finding in the spirit of DeMiguel et al. (2009).

## Sensitivity: rebalance cost (lookback=60 months)

| Cost (bps OW) | 1/N Sharpe | Min-Var | Max-Sharpe | MVO |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 | 1.179 | 1.091 | 1.127 | 1.127 |
| 5.0 | 1.179 | 1.088 | 1.119 | 1.119 |
| 10.0 | 1.179 | 1.084 | 1.111 | 1.111 |
| 20.0 | 1.179 | 1.078 | 1.095 | 1.095 |

1/N is **zero-cost at rebalance** (weights don't change from period to period beyond
drift correction). Every bp of cost widens 1/N's Sharpe advantage over the optimisers.

## The DeMiguel et al. (2009) replication check

The paper found 1/N "cannot be beaten" by any of 14 optimisation strategies across
seven datasets over a 50-year US history. Our post-2018 sector-ETF test replicates
the **directional finding on Sharpe** (1/N leads every optimiser on risk-adjusted
return at every lookback), while showing that raw CAGR can be eeked higher by max-
Sharpe — a distinction the DGU paper notes (they compare out-of-sample Sharpe, not
raw return). On our tiny out-of-sample window (4 years) the results are **statistically
fragile** and should not be over-interpreted.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** 1/N beats all optimisers on Sharpe at every lookback (robust
  finding). Max-Sharpe beats 1/N on raw CAGR in this specific window. The DeMiguel
  et al. result directionally holds but n=4 annual observations is too small for a
  strong claim in either direction.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** 1/N is the cheapest strategy (no estimation, zero-cost
  rebalance). The optimisers are penalised by turnover costs and the short OOS window
  leaves their advantage statistically uncertain (HAC *t* on n=4 is unreliable). The
  sector ETF universe concentrates sector risk; a broader basket might tell a different story.
- **Optimisation is the mirage? — MIXED.** On Sharpe: yes, 1/N wins. On raw CAGR:
  max-Sharpe squeaks ahead. The paper's headline still stands directionally.
